canonicalExplanation.summary: Keyboard users move through a page with **Tab**, in DOM order. If your site menu has 30 links, they must press Tab 30 times on every page to reach the content — unless you add a **skip link**: the first focusable element, `Skip to main content`, which becomes visible on focus and jumps past the menu. Keep the Tab order matching the visual order, and never remove focus outlines without a replacement.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Try it: put your mouse away and press Tab on a big website. Menu item… menu item… 25 presses later, you finally reach the article. For people who navigate only by keyboard or switch device, that's every page, every time. Pressing Tab first reveals Skip to main content, and activating it moves navigation past a long site menu. In this lesson you'll implement and verify a functional skip link and a logical keyboard traversal order.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Sections and landmarks**, **Files, folders and paths**, and **Meaningful links** — a skip link is just a fragment link.

sections.heading: Tab order follows the DOM

includes: Add a skip link that's first, visible on focus and targets main.
Verify Tab order matches visual order and focus stays visible.

outcomes: Implement and verify a functional skip link and logical keyboard traversal order.

examples.title: Skip to main content
examples.situation: Pressing Tab first reveals Skip to main content and activating it moves navigation past a long site menu.
walkthrough: **Pressing Tab first:** focus lands on the hidden skip link, and CSS reveals "Skip to main content".
**Activating it:** Enter follows `#main` and the browser will navigate to it; focus moves to `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">`.
**Next Tab:** the browser will move focus to the first link inside main — navigation has moved past the long site menu.
examples.result: A keyboard user reaches the content in 2 key presses instead of 30.

examples.title: The invisible focus
examples.situation: A site sets `*:focus { outline: none; }` for looks. Keyboard users can't tell where they are.
walkthrough: The skip link and every other link still receive focus, but nothing shows it.
Users lose their place and can't use the page.
Fix: remove that rule, or style `:focus-visible` with a clear outline that matches the design.
examples.result: Focus is always visible, so keyboard users can track their position.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Landmarks make skip links unnecessary for every keyboard user.
misconceptions.correction: Landmark navigation is mainly available through screen readers; sighted keyboard-only users usually can't jump between landmarks. A visible-on-focus skip link helps them bypass repeated menus.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, which users rely on the skip link most?

analogy.example: A skip link is like an **express lane** at the entrance of a supermarket: instead of walking past every shelf to reach the checkout, one sign takes you straight there. It only helps if people can see the sign when they need it.
usefulFor: seeing Tab order as the aisle route
limitations: Supermarkets change aisles; DOM order is your fixed route.
Screen-reader users also have landmark shortcuts — sighted keyboard users don't.

remediation.explanation: Keyboard test ritual: **reload → Tab once (skip link visible?) → Enter (in main?) → keep tabbing (order matches layout? focus always visible?)**.

recap.summary: To implement and verify a functional skip link, make it the first focusable element, hidden until focused, linking to #main with a focusable target. Keep a logical keyboard traversal order by matching DOM order to visual order, and never hide focus.
